newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Massacre victims found as refugees flee Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Massacre victims found as refugees flee Zaire.

text.p: Some 700,000 Hutu refugees abandoned camps in eastern Zaire on Friday and trudged slowly back to Rwanda, leaving behind bodies of women and children hacked to pieces. Fighting with rebels continued.
As night fell, a human tide of refugees moved slowly through the east Zairean town of Goma in the direction of the Rwandan border a few kilometres (miles) away.

The exodus was made possible after an alliance of Zairean rebels, including ethnic Tutsis, drove back Rwandan Hutu militia and ex-government soldiers, breaking their stranglehold on refugees in the teeming wasteland of Mugunga -- the world's largest refugee camp.

"It seems the whole pocket around Goma and Mugunga involving 700,000 plus people is on the move, most of them in this direction. Mugunga camp is completely empty, but we have been discovering massacre sites within the camp," U.N. refugee agency spokesman Ray Wilkinson told reporters in Goma.

"In one area near the Oxfam water tanks we discovered 26 dead people, all women and children apart from one man, macheted to death with their heads split open. Camps are virtually deserted and tens of thousands of rats are reclaiming the camps."
Reporters saw 13 more bodies in a ditch by the road to Goma. One woman had been decapitated and had her arms cut off. She lay in a tangle of bodies and belongings.

Refugees said Tutsi rebels had killed the refugees but this could not be independently confirmed. It was possible that Hutu militiamen, who had taken part in the genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994, had killed some of the Hutu refugees in Mugunga before fleeing westwards.
Witnesses said fighting was continuing west of Mugunga as the rebels pushed the front line further away from Rwanda.
President Bill Clinton told a White House news conference the United States remained prepared to contribute troops to a Zaire relief mission despite the flow of Hutus back to Rwanda.
"The world's most powerful nation must not turn its back on so many desperate people and so many innocent children," he said.

"The mission Canada proposes to lead, and that I believe America should take part in, would provide security for civilian relief agencies to deliver the aid these people must have and to help the refugees who so desire to return home to Rwanda."

Washington announced this week it had agreed tentatively to send 1,000 troops to Goma to secure the airport and set up a protected corridor so refugees could return to Rwanda. Another 3,000 U.S. troops or so would provide support.

In New York British U.N. envoy Sir John Weston said the Security Council agreed during closed-door consultations on a resolution to deploy a multinational force in eastern Zaire and it would be adopted later in the day,
Hutu militia and Rwandan ex-government soldiers had made Mugunga camp a base in exile after fleeing to Zaire in 1994, having slaughtered up to one million Rwandans, mostly Tutsis.
Refugees were held virtual hostage in the camp, intimidated into staying in exile, until the Zairean rebels bombarded the camp on Thursday ahead of the planned arrival of the multinational force.
Mugunga camp was deserted -- burnt, looted and ransacked.
"At this rate, most of these people could be home by the weekend, it is extraordinary we have seen the cracking of this problem in one day," Wilkinson said.
A Reuter correspondent reported the refugees were moving past Mugunga at the rate of 30,000 an hour and were backed up westwards along the road as far as 20 km (12 miles).
The rebels have seized a strip of Zaire along its eastern border in a month of fighting, also involving Zairean forces.

"We left Mugunga an empty camp, we all fled because of the fighting yesterday," said refugee Vincent Nzehsi. "I am going back to Rubavu, Rwanda. There are no militia in the camp, they are all in the forest," he explained.
The exodus was good news for the international community which, wary of the hazards posed in the lawless region, had warned it would not take on the armed Hutus.
The U.N.'s World Food Programme, waiting on the Rwandan side of the border with food, said up to 10,000 had already crossed with a further 275,000 backed up along the road.
Aid organisations have not yet decided whether to shelter the returnees in temporary transit sites or return them directly to their home districts.
Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu, himself a Hutu, went to the Gisenyi border post to welcome his fellow countrymen. He received a tumultuous reception from the refugees.
"We have come here to welcome the people to show them the whole population was waiting for them to reassure them there won't be any harassment. They are welcome in Rwanda," he said.
Asked if he saw a need for foreign intervention now, he replied: "I dont think so. As you can see almost the whole population has come apart from those who are willing to fight."

Rwanda and aid organisations had warned failure to tackle Hutu thugs would risk a re-run of 1994 when they were effectively saved by an international intervention which froze the military situation on the ground.
The Hutu presence has also destabilised eastern Zaire and was a major factor in the rebellion led by Zairean Tutsis against the Zairean army one month ago.
Underlining the volatile nature of the region, Zaire said it would wage war on Burundi and Rwanda which it accuses of violating its territory in fighting in its east.
"We are determined to wage a total war...We have the means," Zairean Deputy Foreign Minister Lokondo Yoka told a news conference in Brussels.
Zaire's ragged army is outnumbered by Rwanda's 54,000-strong force which is dominated by Tutsis who swept the then Hutu-led government from power in 1994 following the genocide.
